subtopics.summary: Background: Coherent spectroscopic or inelastic scattering techniques in the visible and infrared spectral regimes have been extensively exploited for probing chemical and biomolecular phenomena under chemically reactive, biologically active, and non-equilibrium conditions. These methods have been generally restricted to optically thin systems. With the advent of high-intensity extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) and X-ray light sources, there now exists the possibility of interacting with and observing inelastic scattering processes deep within optically thick systems[1].
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Non-linear Mixing Processes for EUV and X-ray Radiation in Optically Thick Systems

subtopics.summary: Background: Traditionally, most electronic materials are characterized as having a single majority carrier type, either electrons or holes, that leads to isotropic n-type or p-type conductivity. These p-type and n-type regions are integrated together to form virtually all modern electronic and energy harvesting devices. Recently, there have been numerous advances in the discovery of single crystalline, goniopolar materials that simultaneously exhibit ntype and p-type conduction behavior along different crystallographic directions. [1-3].
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Tunable Goniopolar Semiconductors

subtopics.summary: Background: Artificial Intelligence (AI), including machine learning, is increasingly pervasive in scientific discovery. But a common question, echoing various refinements of the Turing test, is whether current AI systems are capable of scientific reasoning at the human level.
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Robustness to Novel Queries in AI for Scientific Discovery

subtopics.summary: Background: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ptychography, a powerful computational imaging technique, surpasses the limitations of traditional TEM, offering significant advantages in resolution, electron dose efficiency, and a wide range of applications. Ptychography is a technique that aims to solve the diffractionpattern phase problem (loss of information that can occur when making a physical measurement) by combining multiple diffraction patterns to infer their relative phase and reconstruct a high-resolution image.
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Unlocking the Potential of TEM Ptychography

subtopics.summary: Background: Quantum-level control over energy and matter has been a paradigm of critical significance for current and future science and applications. Over the last several decades, exquisite coherent control has been demonstrated in a vast array of basic platforms, spurring new fields like quantum information science, and applications spanning gravitational wave detection to ultra-precise timing. With the development of new tools, new opportunities have emerged.
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Science with Optical Cycling Centers for Energy Redistribution (SOCCER)

subtopics.summary: Background: Thorium-229, the only nuclear isotope with a known isomer transition at laser-accessible energies, has recently had the frequency of this transition verified to 13 significant figures. This transition has been probed in several solid-state hosts including bulk crystals and thin films, but many open questions remain. For example, the lifetime of the nuclear transition appears to be roughly 4x shorter in Th thin films than in Th-doped bulk crystals.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Th-229 Enabled by the Solid State (TESS)

subtopics.summary: Background: Our evolving ability to exploit some of the more exotic properties of quantum mechanics is poised to reshape computing, sensing, communication, optics and more. Leveraging the fundamental unit of quantum information, the "qubit" is central to many approaches. There are numerous spin-bearing entities that can host a qubit, and molecular systems are intriguing because they can be made reproducibly in large quantities with control over structure and interactions through bottom-up rational design.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Reticular Qubit Assemblies

subtopics.summary: Particulates Background: Bacteria, fungi, and archaea and their metabolic by-products have recently been identified as a significant component of smoke particulate matter. There is increasing evidence that more than seventy percent of these organisms remain viable through fire emission and transport and are capable of colonizing new locations upon deposition, potentially due to biotic-abiotic interactions on the pyrolyzed material. The dissemination of microbes and biological material has important implications for plant, animal, and ecosystem resilience and stability.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Some Like It Hot: Decoding the Biogeochemical Matrix of Fire and Smoke Borne Particulates

subtopics.summary: Background: Recently discovered synthetic superconcentrated electrolytes are enabling unprecedented voltages for energy storage; however, fundamental questions related to unique ion dynamics, coordination, and phase transfer events at a superconcentrated multiphase interface are only beginning to be investigated. Subsea brine pools represent a compelling natural analog, where density and salinity drive phase segregation of seawater and superconcentrated brine to form “underwater lakes”.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Interfacial Superconcentration in Extreme Multiphase Regimes

subtopics.summary: Background: Heterostructures and superlattices of crystalline solids are the platforms upon which modern semiconductor electronics and optoelectronics have been built. Conventionally, integrating solid state materials relies on covalent bonding of the constituent materials but suffers from disorder defects formed due to mismatch which degrades the electronic properties [1]. This restricts such integration into a narrow set of materials with compatible structures.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Atomic and Molecular Hybrid Quantum Solids

subtopics.summary: Background: Over the last few years, generative AI (GenAI) models made impressive advances. They can now solve complex problems and generate original content that we thought only humans could do. Most importantly, they can generate contents that are hard to distinguish from human created contents. For example, this year, a large language model (LLM) reached the level of gold-medal students in the International Mathematical Olympiad [1], and last year an LLM was able to generate novel research ideas that are apparently more creative than the ideas generated by human researchers.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Distinguishing between AI generated content and human created content

subtopics.summary: Background: While many electromagnetic communication methods require line-of-sight propagation, the tropospheric scatter phenomenon facilitates beyond visual horizon transmission of signals via random scattering of radio waves (from around VHF to X-band) in the upper troposphere. Atmospheric turbulence and moisture layers refract much of the signal, causing only a small amount of energy to be received.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Troposcatter Sensitivity to Atmospheric and Electromagnetic Conditions

subtopics.summary: Background: Developing materials capable of guiding biofilm function offers a promising approach to address biofouling, corrosion, remediation, and biohybrid system design. However, we lack a comprehensive understanding of how specific material properties, at the molecular level, influence the recruitment, assembly, and emergent function of diverse biofilms. Current strategies focus on material and biological components separately rather than unraveling the complex interactions of materialbiological interfaces.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Interface Mediated Control of Biofilm Function

subtopics.summary: Background: This MURI will enable unprecedented electrochemical behavior by establishing a fundamental understanding of the multivariate properties that emerge from the interplay of disparate elements in high entropy (HE) materials. High entropy materials (HEMs) leverage enhanced configurational entropy to stabilize single-phase structures comprising ≥5 principal elements, and permit crystal phases to exist outside traditional stability conditions.
subtopics.title: (ONR) High-Entropy Electrochemical Material

subtopics.summary: Background: Additive generation is prevalent in nature: growth from a single cell to a complex organism occurs one cell at a time. Throughout the typical life span of an organism, small and large damage to its structures is inevitable. Organisms have developed varying solutions to mitigate any loss in their structural integrity due to damage. The self-healing (repair) solutions, for example, range from regrowth or repair of damaged tissues in some animal species to growth around damage (compartmentalization) in some tree species.

subtopics.summary: Background: Coherent spectroscopic or inelastic scattering techniques in the visible and infrared spectral regimes have been extensively exploited for probing chemical and biomolecular phenomena under chemically reactive, biologically active, and non-equilibrium conditions. These methods have been generally restricted to optically thin systems. With the advent of high-intensity extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) and X-ray light sources, there now exists the possibility of interacting with and observing inelastic scattering processes deep within optically thick systems[1].
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Non-linear Mixing Processes for EUV and X-ray Radiation in Optically Thick Systems

subtopics.summary: Background: Traditionally, most electronic materials are characterized as having a single majority carrier type, either electrons or holes, that leads to isotropic n-type or p-type conductivity. These p-type and n-type regions are integrated together to form virtually all modern electronic and energy harvesting devices. Recently, there have been numerous advances in the discovery of single crystalline, goniopolar materials that simultaneously exhibit ntype and p-type conduction behavior along different crystallographic directions. [1-3].
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Tunable Goniopolar Semiconductors

subtopics.summary: Background: Artificial Intelligence (AI), including machine learning, is increasingly pervasive in scientific discovery. But a common question, echoing various refinements of the Turing test, is whether current AI systems are capable of scientific reasoning at the human level.
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Robustness to Novel Queries in AI for Scientific Discovery

subtopics.summary: Background: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ptychography, a powerful computational imaging technique, surpasses the limitations of traditional TEM, offering significant advantages in resolution, electron dose efficiency, and a wide range of applications. Ptychography is a technique that aims to solve the diffractionpattern phase problem (loss of information that can occur when making a physical measurement) by combining multiple diffraction patterns to infer their relative phase and reconstruct a high-resolution image.
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Unlocking the Potential of TEM Ptychography

subtopics.summary: Background: Quantum-level control over energy and matter has been a paradigm of critical significance for current and future science and applications. Over the last several decades, exquisite coherent control has been demonstrated in a vast array of basic platforms, spurring new fields like quantum information science, and applications spanning gravitational wave detection to ultra-precise timing. With the development of new tools, new opportunities have emerged.
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Science with Optical Cycling Centers for Energy Redistribution (SOCCER)

subtopics.summary: Background: Thorium-229, the only nuclear isotope with a known isomer transition at laser-accessible energies, has recently had the frequency of this transition verified to 13 significant figures. This transition has been probed in several solid-state hosts including bulk crystals and thin films, but many open questions remain. For example, the lifetime of the nuclear transition appears to be roughly 4x shorter in Th thin films than in Th-doped bulk crystals.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Th-229 Enabled by the Solid State (TESS)

subtopics.summary: Background: Our evolving ability to exploit some of the more exotic properties of quantum mechanics is poised to reshape computing, sensing, communication, optics and more. Leveraging the fundamental unit of quantum information, the "qubit" is central to many approaches. There are numerous spin-bearing entities that can host a qubit, and molecular systems are intriguing because they can be made reproducibly in large quantities with control over structure and interactions through bottom-up rational design.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Reticular Qubit Assemblies

subtopics.summary: Particulates Background: Bacteria, fungi, and archaea and their metabolic by-products have recently been identified as a significant component of smoke particulate matter. There is increasing evidence that more than seventy percent of these organisms remain viable through fire emission and transport and are capable of colonizing new locations upon deposition, potentially due to biotic-abiotic interactions on the pyrolyzed material. The dissemination of microbes and biological material has important implications for plant, animal, and ecosystem resilience and stability.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Some Like It Hot: Decoding the Biogeochemical Matrix of Fire and Smoke Borne Particulates

subtopics.summary: Background: Recently discovered synthetic superconcentrated electrolytes are enabling unprecedented voltages for energy storage; however, fundamental questions related to unique ion dynamics, coordination, and phase transfer events at a superconcentrated multiphase interface are only beginning to be investigated. Subsea brine pools represent a compelling natural analog, where density and salinity drive phase segregation of seawater and superconcentrated brine to form “underwater lakes”.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Interfacial Superconcentration in Extreme Multiphase Regimes

subtopics.summary: Background: Heterostructures and superlattices of crystalline solids are the platforms upon which modern semiconductor electronics and optoelectronics have been built. Conventionally, integrating solid state materials relies on covalent bonding of the constituent materials but suffers from disorder defects formed due to mismatch which degrades the electronic properties [1]. This restricts such integration into a narrow set of materials with compatible structures.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Atomic and Molecular Hybrid Quantum Solids

subtopics.summary: Background: Over the last few years, generative AI (GenAI) models made impressive advances. They can now solve complex problems and generate original content that we thought only humans could do. Most importantly, they can generate contents that are hard to distinguish from human created contents. For example, this year, a large language model (LLM) reached the level of gold-medal students in the International Mathematical Olympiad [1], and last year an LLM was able to generate novel research ideas that are apparently more creative than the ideas generated by human researchers.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Distinguishing between AI generated content and human created content

subtopics.summary: Background: While many electromagnetic communication methods require line-of-sight propagation, the tropospheric scatter phenomenon facilitates beyond visual horizon transmission of signals via random scattering of radio waves (from around VHF to X-band) in the upper troposphere. Atmospheric turbulence and moisture layers refract much of the signal, causing only a small amount of energy to be received.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Troposcatter Sensitivity to Atmospheric and Electromagnetic Conditions

subtopics.summary: Background: Developing materials capable of guiding biofilm function offers a promising approach to address biofouling, corrosion, remediation, and biohybrid system design. However, we lack a comprehensive understanding of how specific material properties, at the molecular level, influence the recruitment, assembly, and emergent function of diverse biofilms. Current strategies focus on material and biological components separately rather than unraveling the complex interactions of materialbiological interfaces.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Interface Mediated Control of Biofilm Function

subtopics.summary: Background: This MURI will enable unprecedented electrochemical behavior by establishing a fundamental understanding of the multivariate properties that emerge from the interplay of disparate elements in high entropy (HE) materials. High entropy materials (HEMs) leverage enhanced configurational entropy to stabilize single-phase structures comprising ≥5 principal elements, and permit crystal phases to exist outside traditional stability conditions.
subtopics.title: (ONR) High-Entropy Electrochemical Material

subtopics.summary: Background: Additive generation is prevalent in nature: growth from a single cell to a complex organism occurs one cell at a time. Throughout the typical life span of an organism, small and large damage to its structures is inevitable. Organisms have developed varying solutions to mitigate any loss in their structural integrity due to damage. The self-healing (repair) solutions, for example, range from regrowth or repair of damaged tissues in some animal species to growth around damage (compartmentalization) in some tree species.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Bio-Inspired Autonomous and Recurrent Self-Healing in Materials and Structures

subtopics.summary: Background: Coherent spectroscopic or inelastic scattering techniques in the visible and infrared spectral regimes have been extensively exploited for probing chemical and biomolecular phenomena under chemically reactive, biologically active, and non-equilibrium conditions. These methods have been generally restricted to optically thin systems. With the advent of high-intensity extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) and X-ray light sources, there now exists the possibility of interacting with and observing inelastic scattering processes deep within optically thick systems[1].
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Non-linear Mixing Processes for EUV and X-ray Radiation in Optically Thick Systems

subtopics.summary: Background: Traditionally, most electronic materials are characterized as having a single majority carrier type, either electrons or holes, that leads to isotropic n-type or p-type conductivity. These p-type and n-type regions are integrated together to form virtually all modern electronic and energy harvesting devices. Recently, there have been numerous advances in the discovery of single crystalline, goniopolar materials that simultaneously exhibit ntype and p-type conduction behavior along different crystallographic directions. [1-3].
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Tunable Goniopolar Semiconductors

subtopics.summary: Background: Artificial Intelligence (AI), including machine learning, is increasingly pervasive in scientific discovery. But a common question, echoing various refinements of the Turing test, is whether current AI systems are capable of scientific reasoning at the human level.
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Robustness to Novel Queries in AI for Scientific Discovery

subtopics.summary: Background: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ptychography, a powerful computational imaging technique, surpasses the limitations of traditional TEM, offering significant advantages in resolution, electron dose efficiency, and a wide range of applications. Ptychography is a technique that aims to solve the diffractionpattern phase problem (loss of information that can occur when making a physical measurement) by combining multiple diffraction patterns to infer their relative phase and reconstruct a high-resolution image.
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Unlocking the Potential of TEM Ptychography

subtopics.summary: Background: Quantum-level control over energy and matter has been a paradigm of critical significance for current and future science and applications. Over the last several decades, exquisite coherent control has been demonstrated in a vast array of basic platforms, spurring new fields like quantum information science, and applications spanning gravitational wave detection to ultra-precise timing. With the development of new tools, new opportunities have emerged.
subtopics.title: (AFOSR) Science with Optical Cycling Centers for Energy Redistribution (SOCCER)

subtopics.summary: Background: Thorium-229, the only nuclear isotope with a known isomer transition at laser-accessible energies, has recently had the frequency of this transition verified to 13 significant figures. This transition has been probed in several solid-state hosts including bulk crystals and thin films, but many open questions remain. For example, the lifetime of the nuclear transition appears to be roughly 4x shorter in Th thin films than in Th-doped bulk crystals.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Th-229 Enabled by the Solid State (TESS)

subtopics.summary: Background: Our evolving ability to exploit some of the more exotic properties of quantum mechanics is poised to reshape computing, sensing, communication, optics and more. Leveraging the fundamental unit of quantum information, the "qubit" is central to many approaches. There are numerous spin-bearing entities that can host a qubit, and molecular systems are intriguing because they can be made reproducibly in large quantities with control over structure and interactions through bottom-up rational design.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Reticular Qubit Assemblies

subtopics.summary: Particulates Background: Bacteria, fungi, and archaea and their metabolic by-products have recently been identified as a significant component of smoke particulate matter. There is increasing evidence that more than seventy percent of these organisms remain viable through fire emission and transport and are capable of colonizing new locations upon deposition, potentially due to biotic-abiotic interactions on the pyrolyzed material. The dissemination of microbes and biological material has important implications for plant, animal, and ecosystem resilience and stability.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Some Like It Hot: Decoding the Biogeochemical Matrix of Fire and Smoke Borne Particulates

subtopics.summary: Background: Recently discovered synthetic superconcentrated electrolytes are enabling unprecedented voltages for energy storage; however, fundamental questions related to unique ion dynamics, coordination, and phase transfer events at a superconcentrated multiphase interface are only beginning to be investigated. Subsea brine pools represent a compelling natural analog, where density and salinity drive phase segregation of seawater and superconcentrated brine to form “underwater lakes”.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Interfacial Superconcentration in Extreme Multiphase Regimes

subtopics.summary: Background: Heterostructures and superlattices of crystalline solids are the platforms upon which modern semiconductor electronics and optoelectronics have been built. Conventionally, integrating solid state materials relies on covalent bonding of the constituent materials but suffers from disorder defects formed due to mismatch which degrades the electronic properties [1]. This restricts such integration into a narrow set of materials with compatible structures.
subtopics.title: (ARO) Atomic and Molecular Hybrid Quantum Solids

subtopics.summary: Background: Over the last few years, generative AI (GenAI) models made impressive advances. They can now solve complex problems and generate original content that we thought only humans could do. Most importantly, they can generate contents that are hard to distinguish from human created contents. For example, this year, a large language model (LLM) reached the level of gold-medal students in the International Mathematical Olympiad [1], and last year an LLM was able to generate novel research ideas that are apparently more creative than the ideas generated by human researchers.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Distinguishing between AI generated content and human created content

subtopics.summary: Background: While many electromagnetic communication methods require line-of-sight propagation, the tropospheric scatter phenomenon facilitates beyond visual horizon transmission of signals via random scattering of radio waves (from around VHF to X-band) in the upper troposphere. Atmospheric turbulence and moisture layers refract much of the signal, causing only a small amount of energy to be received.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Troposcatter Sensitivity to Atmospheric and Electromagnetic Conditions

subtopics.summary: Background: Developing materials capable of guiding biofilm function offers a promising approach to address biofouling, corrosion, remediation, and biohybrid system design. However, we lack a comprehensive understanding of how specific material properties, at the molecular level, influence the recruitment, assembly, and emergent function of diverse biofilms. Current strategies focus on material and biological components separately rather than unraveling the complex interactions of materialbiological interfaces.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Interface Mediated Control of Biofilm Function

subtopics.summary: Background: This MURI will enable unprecedented electrochemical behavior by establishing a fundamental understanding of the multivariate properties that emerge from the interplay of disparate elements in high entropy (HE) materials. High entropy materials (HEMs) leverage enhanced configurational entropy to stabilize single-phase structures comprising ≥5 principal elements, and permit crystal phases to exist outside traditional stability conditions.
subtopics.title: (ONR) High-Entropy Electrochemical Material

subtopics.summary: Background: Additive generation is prevalent in nature: growth from a single cell to a complex organism occurs one cell at a time. Throughout the typical life span of an organism, small and large damage to its structures is inevitable. Organisms have developed varying solutions to mitigate any loss in their structural integrity due to damage. The self-healing (repair) solutions, for example, range from regrowth or repair of damaged tissues in some animal species to growth around damage (compartmentalization) in some tree species.
subtopics.title: (ONR) Bio-Inspired Autonomous and Recurrent Self-Healing in Materials and Structures

subtopics.summary: Website: https://science.osti.gov/ascr/Research/Applied-Mathematics This subprogram supports basic research leading to fundamental mathematical advances and computational breakthroughs across DOE and SC missions.
subtopics.title: (a) Applied Mathematics

subtopics.summary: Website: https://science.osti.gov/ascr/Research/Computer-Science This subprogram supports research that advances computing and networking at extreme scales (i.e., exascale computing, massively parallelism, big data) and the understanding of extreme scale, or complex data from both simulations and experiments. The subprogram aims to make high performance scientific computers and networks highly productive and efficient to solve scientific challenges while attempting to reduce domain science application complexity as much as possible.
subtopics.title: (b) Computer Science

subtopics.summary: Website: https://science.osti.gov/ascr/Research/scidac This activity primarily supports the Scientific Discovery through Advanced Computing (SciDAC), program, which is a recognized leader in employing HPC for scientific discovery. Established in 2001, SciDAC involves ASCR partnerships with the other SC programs, other DOE program offices, and other Federal agencies in strategic areas. The goal is to dramatically accelerate progress in scientific computing through strong collaborations between discipline scientists, applied mathematicians, and computer scientists.
subtopics.title: (c) Computational Partnerships

subtopics.summary: Website: https://science.osti.gov/ascr/ This activity supports research and evaluation of prototypes (REP), including AI infrastructures, classical and quantum computing and networking. The REP activity addresses the challenges of next-generation technologies. By actively partnering with the research community, including industry and Federal agencies, on developing technologies that enable next-generation machines, ASCR ensures that commercially available architectures serve the needs of the scientific community.
subtopics.title: (d) Advanced Computing Technologies

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports hypothesis-driven research on materials and focuses on the roles of chemical reactivity, chemical transformation, and chemical dynamics on the material composition, structure, function, and lifetime across the range of length scales from atomic to mesoscopic. Common themes include discovering the mechanistic detail for chemical synthesis, transformations, and dynamics of materials; fundamental understanding of structure-property relationships of functional materials; and using chemistry to control interfacial properties and interactions between materials.
subtopics.title: (a) Materials Chemistry

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports fundamental materials science research for discovery, design and synthesis of functional materials based on principles and concepts of biology. Nature provides a blueprint for organizing and manipulating matter, energy, entropy, and information across multiple length scales to build material systems that display complex yet well-coordinated collective behavior.
subtopics.title: (b) Biomolecular Materials

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports research to understand the physical phenomena and unifying principles that govern materials synthesis and processing across multiple length scales. Key phenomena of interest include diffusion, nucleation, and phase transitions, as well as the role interfaces and defects play in the emergence of materials functionality.
subtopics.title: (c) Synthesis and Processing Science

subtopics.summary: The Experimental Condensed Matter Physics (ECMP) subprogram supports research that advances our fundamental understanding of the quantum physics governing the electronic structure of complex solid materials and will allow us to achieve new materials functionalities by manipulating and controlling collective excitations and quasiparticles. For this funding cycle, ECMP encourages the submission of applications that address quantitative probes of many-body quantum correlations and collective states in quantum materials.
subtopics.title: (d) Experimental Condensed Matter Physics

subtopics.summary: The Theoretical Condensed Matter Physics (TCMP) subprogram supports fundamental research in theoretical condensed matter physics to advance our understanding of quantum materials, drive materials discovery and design, and pioneer novel materials theories aligned with the DOE mission. The subprogram funds transformative research predicting and interpreting emerging quantum phenomena and out-of-equilibrium quantum dynamics, including driven and many-body systems.
subtopics.title: (e) Theoretical Condensed Matter Physics

subtopics.summary: The Physical Behavior of Materials (PBM) subprogram supports basic research that aims to advance our fundamental understanding and control of the processes and interactions that determine the physical behavior of materials. It supports studies of how materials respond to external stimuli, such as temperature, pressure, electromagnetic fields, and strain. Also of interest are the influence of defects, disorder, heterogeneity, surfaces, and interfaces on the physical behavior of materials.
subtopics.title: (f) Physical Behavior of Materials

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports basic research to understand defects in materials and their effects on the properties such as strength, structure, deformation, and failure. Defect formation, growth, migration, and propagation are examined by coordinated experimental and modeling efforts over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales as well as a range of environments and stimuli.
subtopics.title: (g) Mechanical Behavior and Radiation Effects

subtopics.subtopic_code: (h) Quantum Information Science in Materials Sciences and Engineering
subtopics.summary: This research subprogram focuses on Materials Sciences and Engineering, investigating the fundamental material properties that are essential for QIS and enable advanced QIS technologies. Within the Basic Energy Sciences, this subprogram crosscuts the three MSE Division research areas: Materials Discovery, Design, and Synthesis; Condensed Matter and Materials Physics; and Scattering and Instrumentation Sciences.
subtopics.title: (h) Quantum Information Science in Materials Sciences and Engineering

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports basic research on the fundamental interactions of photons with matter to achieve an understanding of atomic, electronic, and magnetic structures and excitations and their relationships to materials properties, including the dynamics of quantum phenomena. The main emphasis is on x-ray scattering, spectroscopy, and imaging research, primarily at major BES-supported user facilities. Instrumentation development and experimental research in ultrafast materials science, across the full electromagnetic spectrum, is an integral part of the portfolio.
subtopics.title: (i) X-Ray Scattering

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports hypothesis-driven research to understand atomic, molecular, electronics, and magnetic structures and excitations, and their relationships to macroscopic properties, including mechanical, thermal, electronic, magnetic, and topological. Neutron scattering, spectroscopy, and imaging research performed primarily at DOE neutron facilities should be central to this research. The scientific research should use advances in neutron scattering driven by improved source performance, instrumentation, and advanced data acquisition and analysis approaches.
subtopics.title: (j) Neutron Scattering

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports basic research in materials sciences using advanced electron and scanning probe microscopy and related spectroscopy techniques to understand the atomic, electronic, and magnetic structures and properties of materials. This activity also supports the development of new instrumentation concepts and quantitative techniques to advance materials characterizations. Supported advancements include ultrafast electron diffraction and imaging techniques.
subtopics.title: (k) Electron and Scanning Probe Microscopies

subtopics.summary: The Ultrafast Molecular and Optical Sciences (UMOS) subprogram supports fundamental experimental and theoretical research in ultrafast chemical sciences. The subprogram's primary mission is to establish the foundational knowledge required to control chemical transformations by developing accurate quantum chemical descriptions of excited-state physical and chemical processes and by advancing novel optical tools to guide reactants towards desired products.
subtopics.title: (l)  Ultrafast Molecular and Optical Sciences

subtopics.summary: Research in the Gas Phase Chemical Physics (GPCP) subprogram is pursued through three primary thrust areas. These areas represent distinct yet complementary approaches to understanding and controlling gas-phase chemical phenomena. The thrusts are: Fundamental Chemical Reactivity, which focuses on elementary processes; Emergent Complexity and Systems Chemistry, which addresses collective behaviors in large molecular systems and ensembles; and Gas-Surface Chemical Physics, which targets surface-mediated reactions.
subtopics.title: (m) Gas Phase Chemical Physics

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports fundamental research for the sustained development, innovation, and integration5 of theoretical and computational approaches for the accurate and efficient prediction of chemical processes and mechanisms relevant to the DOE mission. Part of the focus is on simulating dynamical processes that are so complex that efficient computational implementation must be accomplished along with developing new theories and algorithms.
subtopics.title: (n) Computational and Theoretical Chemistry

subtopics.subtopic_code: (o) Condensed Phase and Interfacial Molecular Science
subtopics.summary: The Condensed Phase and Interfacial Molecular Science (CPIMS) subprogram emphasizes basic research at the boundary of chemistry and physics, pursuing a molecular-level understanding of chemical and physical processes in liquids and/or at interfaces. With its foundation in chemical physics, the impact of this crosscutting subprogram is far reaching, providing scientific foundations underpinning a variety of areas of importance to the DOE, including energy, chemical synthesis and manufacturing, microelectronics, nuclear power generation, and quantum information science.
subtopics.title: (o) Condensed Phase and Interfacial Molecular Science

subtopics.summary: The Molecular Quantum Information Science (mQIS) subprogram supports theoretical, computational, and experimental research that advances the quantum information science of complex chemical systems. Efforts in this area develop a fundamental understanding of the structure, dynamics, and control of quantum information processes at the molecular scale, building the scientific foundations for the next generation of molecular quantum technologies in computing, communication, and sensing.
subtopics.title: (p) Molecular Quantum Information Science

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports basic research pursuing novel catalyst design and molecularlevel control of chemical transformations relevant to the conversion of energy resources. Emphasis is on the understanding reaction mechanisms and enabling precise identification and manipulation of catalytic active sites, their environments, and reaction conditions for optimized efficiency and selectivity. Understanding catalytic reaction mechanisms in varied chemical environments and the structure-reactivity relationships of solid and molecular catalysts is a central component of the subprogram.
subtopics.title: (q) Catalysis Science

subtopics.summary: This subprogram provides mechanistic and molecular insight into chemical separation processes or phenomena by supporting fundamental, testable hypothesis-based experimental and computational research questions. Research projects seek to develop foundational knowledge that enable prediction and control of chemical and physical mass transport and phase de-mixing. This research includes understanding the kinetics, thermodynamics, and interfacial dynamics of these transitions across multiple length and time scales, from quantum interactions to macroscopic phenomena.
subtopics.title: (r) Separation Science

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports actinide and transactinide fundamental chemical research that underpins the DOE missions in energy, environment, and national security with an emphasis on the chemical and physical properties of the transuranic elements. The unique molecular bonding of these elements is explored using experiment and theory to elucidate electronic and molecular structure, reaction thermodynamics, as well as quantum phenomena.
subtopics.title: (s) Heavy Element Chemistry

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports basic experimental, theoretical, and computational research in geochemistry and geophysics that have clear connections to energy production or recovering critical elements. Geochemical research emphasizes fundamental understanding of the reaction mechanisms and rates associated with geochemical processes, focusing on molecular-mesoscale aspects of minerals and interfaces and on the molecular origins of critical element distributions and their influence on migration, separation, or fractionation pathways in the earth.
subtopics.title: (t) Geosciences

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports fundamental, molecular-level research on photochemistry and radiation chemistry in the condensed phase and at interfaces. Photochemical processes initiated by absorbing visible or near-infrared light may ultimately form the basis of reliable, secure energy technologies that generate energy-rich chemicals or electricity. Advances in these areas will require a thorough understanding of elementary processes such as light absorption, charge separation, and charge transport within a number of chemical systems, including those with significant nanostructured composition.
subtopics.title: (u) Photochemistry and Radiation Chemistry

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports basic research on the capture and conversion of solar energy to chemical energy in the photosynthetic systems of plants, algae, and photosynthetic microbes. Topics of study include, but are not limited to, light harvesting, proton and electron transport, reduction of carbon dioxide to form organic compounds, and the self-assembly and self-repair of photosynthetic proteins, complexes and membranes.
subtopics.title: (v) Photosynthetic Systems

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports basic research into the biochemistry, biophysics, and molecular biology that underpins natural energy capture, conversion, and storage systems.
subtopics.title: (w) Physical Biosciences

subtopics.summary: This subprogram supports research that advances the instruments, techniques, and capabilities of the existing and/or future scientific user facilities. Of interest is research that aims at developing techniques that will enable and/or strongly benefit the next generation of accelerator-based particle sources. Research includes studies of creating, manipulating, and transporting ultrahigh brightness beams and modeling of beam dynamics.
subtopics.title: (x) BES Accelerator and Detector Research

subtopics.summary: BER’s Microbial Biosystems Design seeks to gain a fundamental understanding of genome-encoded functions in microbes and microbiomes and to design and engineer new biological processes for energy and the economy, providing the basic science to strengthen U.S. leadership in biotechnology innovation. Microbial Biosystems Design is advancing towards a robust and secure U.S.
subtopics.title: (a) Microbial Biosystems Design

subtopics.subtopic_code: (b) Classical and Quantum-Enabled Bioimaging and Sensing
subtopics.summary: BER’s Bioimaging Science supports integrative approaches to detect, visualize, and measure biological processes in situ to gain a predictive understanding of cellular function. To support advanced genomics research and the foundations of biotechnology development, the Bioimaging program encourages developing new imaging instrumentation and technologies for studying cellular and molecular systems and networks critical to research on DOE-relevant plants, microbes, and microbial communities.
subtopics.title: (b) Classical and Quantum-Enabled Bioimaging and Sensing

subtopics.summary: The U.S. population is continuously exposed to low-dose and low-dose-rate ionizing radiation (IR) from several different sources, including natural background sources, medical applications, and occupational exposures. BER’s Low Dose Radiation Research seeks to take advantage of advanced model systems, high throughput genomics and other multi-omics approaches, and computational AI/ML tools and technologies to advance a more mechanistic understanding of low dose and low dose rate radiation effects on cellular metabolism.
subtopics.title: (c) Low Dose Radiation Research

subtopics.subtopic_code: (a) Theory, Simulation, and Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
subtopics.summary: The Theory, Simulation, and AI/ML subprogram supports efforts to close critical scientific and technology gaps in advancing fusion energy as described in the Roadmap through foundational theory, first-principles, high-performance computing, and data-driven methodologies. Supported activities span the full range of other FES fusion-relevant subprogram areas, including developing fusion data resources, advanced simulations, AI models, and scientific software frameworks.
subtopics.title: (a) Theory, Simulation, and Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning

subtopics.summary: Developing materials suitable for a power-producing fusion device is prerequisite for the eventual success of fusion power. Every component, from the innermost chamber walls to the outer framework, demands materials that can endure and perform in demanding conditions, including extremes of heat, particle exposure, and neutron fluxes. The Fusion Materials and Internal Components (FM&IC) subprogram is devoted to advancing materials, developing physical and numerical material models, and realizing essential material tools necessary to achieve fusion power.
subtopics.title: (b) Fusion Materials and Internal Components

subtopics.summary: The Toroidal Long Pulse (TLP) area addresses gaps in the physics and technology basis for the conventional tokamak and stellarator approaches to magnetic confinement fusion. The TLP Tokamak Research area includes research on the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in San Diego, CA, small-scale tokamak research conducted on university-scale devices, and research on international tokamak facilities accessible to U.S. staff under international bilateral agreements and multi-lateral frameworks.
subtopics.title: (c) Toroidal Long Pulse

subtopics.summary: The Compact Toroidal Concepts subprogram supports research needed to develop a compact toroidal configuration. Two promising concepts are the spherical tokamak (ST), such as the National Spherical Torus Experimental-Upgrade (NSTX-U), and conventional aspect ratio tokamaks operated at high toroidal magnetic fields, exemplified by the SPARC tokamak. These devices offer complementary strategies for improving confinement and achieving compactness: STs use enhanced plasma physics properties while high-field conventional tokamaks rely on high-field magnets.
subtopics.title: (d) Compact Toroidal Concepts

subtopics.summary: The Inertial Fusion Energy (IFE) subprogram is dedicated to advancing the foundational science and technology essential for developing IFE as a viable energy source. Key research areas of interest are outlined in the IFE Basic Research Needs Workshop Report. In addition, the FES program has established IFE Science and Technology hubs, which focus on both scientific advancement and the stewardship of the IFE ecosystem. We encourage applications that use this ecosystem.
subtopics.title: (e) Inertial Fusion Energy

subtopics.summary: The Innovate part of the Build-Innovate-Grow strategy in the Roadmap includes support of Measurement Innovation (MI) to enable verification and validation of design modelling codes for components and materials under extreme prototypical fusion environmental conditions. The MI subprogram supports the development of world-leading transformative and innovative diagnostic techniques and their application to support both fusion science and technology objectives.
subtopics.title: (f) Measurement Innovation

subtopics.subtopic_code: (g) Closing the Fusion Cycle: Fusion Nuclear Science
subtopics.summary: Applications for the Fusion Nuclear Science (FNS) research activities in the four subprogram areas below may be submitted to this NOFO. The FNS program will conduct yearly comparative merit reviews for both new and renewal applications. We strongly encourage preapplications to ensure alignment with program goals. Before submission, we highly encourage you to contact the subprogram contact for format and content.
subtopics.title: (g) Closing the Fusion Cycle: Fusion Nuclear Science

subtopics.subtopic_code: (h) Closing the Fusion Cycle:  Enabling Research and Development
subtopics.summary: The Enabling Research and Development subprogram establishes the scientific and technological foundation necessary for developing essential components across a wide range of concepts that will eventually be integrated into a fusion energy system. This subprogram addresses many cross-cutting challenges as part of the Innovate portion of the Roadmap’s BuildInnovate-Grow strategy. Enabling R&D supports early-stage, high-impact research.
subtopics.title: (h) Closing the Fusion Cycle:  Enabling Research and Development

subtopics.subtopic_code: (i) Plasma Science and Technology — General Plasma Science
subtopics.summary: The General Plasma Science (GPS) subprogram supports research at the frontiers of foundational plasma science. GPS supports hypothesis-driven, frontier-level research to significantly increase our understanding of the plasma processes spanning magnetic reconnection, turbulence, and dusty plasma. Applicants are strongly encouraged to develop integrated research projects in frontier plasma science, using existing laboratory-based, GPS collaborative research facilities, and high-performance computing.
subtopics.title: (i) Plasma Science and Technology — General Plasma Science

subtopics.subtopic_code: (j) Plasma Science and Technology — High Energy Density Physics
subtopics.summary: The HEDP subprogram seeks to understand how matter behaves under extreme conditions of temperature and pressure. In this domain, energy density is typically defined as being above 1 Mbar (100 GPa or approximately 1 million atmospheres), which is comparable to the energy density of a chemical bond, such as in a water molecule. HEDP conditions are crucial for studying processes such as the formation and destruction of stars and for controlling fusion in laboratory settings. Topics of interest for this NOFO include but are not limited to the following areas.
subtopics.title: (j) Plasma Science and Technology — High Energy Density Physics

subtopics.subtopic_code: (k) Plasma Science and Technology — Microelectronics Research
subtopics.summary: Plasmas are essential to manufacturing devices in the semiconductor industry, from creating extreme ultraviolet photons used in the most advanced lithography to thin film etching, deposition, and surface modifications. An estimated 40–45% of all process steps needed to manufacture semiconductor devices use low temperature plasmas (LTPs) in one form or another. LTPs have been an enabling technology in the multi-decade progression of shrinking device dimensions, often referred to as Moore’s Law.
subtopics.title: (k) Plasma Science and Technology — Microelectronics Research

subtopics.subtopic_code: (l) Plasma Science and Technology — Quantum Information Science
subtopics.summary: The QIS subprogram supports basic research in QIS that could transform FES mission areas and research that takes advantage of unique FES-enabled plasma capabilities to advance QIS development.
subtopics.title: (l) Plasma Science and Technology — Quantum Information Science

subtopics.subtopic_code: (a) Experimental Research at the Energy Frontier in High Energy Physics
subtopics.summary: This research subprogram seeks to support studies of fundamental particles and their interactions using particle beam collisions at the highest possible energies and/or luminosities. This research is accomplished through direct detection of new phenomena or through sensitive measurements of processes that probe the Standard Model and new physics beyond it. In particular, HENP is looking for applications for physics research utilizing data being collected at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) by the ATLAS (A Toroidal LHC Apparatus) and CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) experiments.
subtopics.title: (a) Experimental Research at the Energy Frontier in High Energy Physics

subtopics.subtopic_code: (b) Experimental Research at the Intensity Frontier in High Energy Physics
subtopics.summary: This research area seeks to support precision studies that are sensitive to new physical processes at very high-energy scales, beyond what can be directly probed with energy frontier colliders, and often require intense particle beams.
subtopics.title: (b) Experimental Research at the Intensity Frontier in High Energy Physics

subtopics.subtopic_code: (c) Experimental Research at the Cosmic Frontier in High Energy Physics
subtopics.summary: This research area seeks to support precision studies using observations of the cosmos and naturally occurring cosmic particles to understand the properties of fundamental particles and fields. Priorities include the study of cosmic acceleration by studying the nature of dark energy, planning the next-generation ground-based cosmic microwave background experiment to explore the inflationary epoch, and using direct-detection experiments to search for dark matter particles. Many of the experiments in the program also place constraints on neutrino masses.
subtopics.title: (c) Experimental Research at the Cosmic Frontier in High Energy Physics

subtopics.subtopic_code: (d) Theoretical Research in High Energy Physics
subtopics.summary: This research area seeks to support theoretical activities that provide the vision and the mathematical framework for understanding and extending our knowledge of particles, forces, space-time, and the universe. Theoretical research is essential to support current experiments at the Energy, Intensity, and Cosmic Frontiers to identify new directions for high energy physics and to provide a deeper understanding of nature.
subtopics.title: (d) Theoretical Research in High Energy Physics

subtopics.summary: The nuclear theory subprogram focuses on theory as a fundamental pillar of modern science and nuclear physics. It explains how fundamental building blocks of matter, such as quarks and gluons, combine to form atomic nuclei. It describes how nuclei decay and reacts to release energy, produce various isotopes, and forge chemical elements within stars and stellar explosions. By revealing how nuclear properties unveil fundamental particles and forces, supported nuclear theory research delivers the core concepts, methods, and predictive tools needed to bridge subatomic and astrophysical scales.
subtopics.title: (e) Theoretical Research in Nuclear Physics

subtopics.subtopic_code: (f) Accelerator Science and Technology R&D in High Energy and Nuclear Physics
subtopics.summary: The Accelerator Science and Technology R&D subprogram develops the next generation of particle accelerators and related technologies that are essential for discoveries in high energy physics. This research area supports world-leading research in the physics of charged particle beams, and long-range, early-stage exploratory research aimed at developing new acceleration concepts. In addition, this subprogram also provides graduate and postdoctoral research training, equipment for experiments, test facilities and related computational efforts.
subtopics.title: (f) Accelerator Science and Technology R&D in High Energy and Nuclear Physics

subtopics.subtopic_code: (g) Instrumentation and Detector R&D in High Energy and Nuclear Physics
subtopics.summary: The Detector R&D subprogram develops the next generation of instrumentation for high energy and nuclear physics. It supports research leading to fundamental advances in the science of particle and radiation detection, and the development of new experimental techniques. This research is typically long-term, “generic” R&D that is high-risk but has the potential for wide applicability or high impact. Applications should broadly align with the priority research directions identified in the 2020 DOE Basic Research Needs Study on High Energy Physics Detector Research and Development report.
subtopics.title: (g) Instrumentation and Detector R&D in High Energy and Nuclear Physics

subtopics.subtopic_code: (h) Computational Research in High Energy Physics
subtopics.summary: This research area supports advanced computing research and development targeting challenges that can or could be broadly applied to the increasingly complex high energy physics computing ecosystem. These challenges may include hardware-software co-design, development of collaborative software infrastructure, and research into high-performance software and algorithms. This subprogram facilitates the effective use of DOE computing resources including, high-performance computing and the Genesis Mission American Science and Security Platform.
subtopics.title: (h) Computational Research in High Energy Physics

subtopics.subtopic_code: (i) Quantum Information Science for High Energy Physics Research
subtopics.summary: QIS is the study of how the unique behaviors of the microscopic world described by quantum mechanics — such as entanglement, superposition, and interference — can be used to solve scientific problems and build new technologies, such as quantum sensors and computers. This program pursues the potential for QIS to solve previously intractable problems, measure previously undetectable signals, and bring new theoretical tools to bear on our understanding of the universe through our Quantum Information Science Enabled Discovery (QuantISED) program. This research area is aligned to the SC and U.S.
subtopics.title: (i) Quantum Information Science for High Energy Physics Research

subtopics.subtopic_code: (j) Quantum Information Science for Nuclear Physics Research
subtopics.summary: This pioneering effort has a primary objective of advancing discovery science at the intersection of nuclear physics and QIS. By identifying and coordinating emerging research and applied challenges in both fields, and by using the interdisciplinary nature of quantum computing and QIS, this program creates new opportunities to address complex problems, expanding the frontiers of HENP-supported research and fostering innovation vital for scientific advancement. Successful applications should address at least one of the following topics.
subtopics.title: (j) Quantum Information Science for Nuclear Physics Research

subtopics.summary: Program website: https://science.osti.gov/ardap The Accelerator Stewardship and Accelerator Development subprograms (collectively referred to as Accelerator Stewardship and formerly known as ARDAP) share a mission to: • Coordinate accelerator R&D within the SC • Advance accelerator science and technology relevant to the DOE, other Federal agencies, and U.S.
subtopics.title: (k) Accelerator Stewardship and Accelerator Development

subtopics.summary: The Experimental QCD subprogram is dedicated to: a) unraveling the fundamental nature of matter, specifically focusing on hadrons and, b) focusing on studies of emerging phenomena in the bulk, condensed quark-gluon matter created at extremely high densities and temperatures characteristic of the infant Universe. The study of the hadron structure was previously covered by the Medium Energy (ME) subprogram.
subtopics.title: (l) Experimental QCD

subtopics.summary: The Nuclear Structure and Nuclear Astrophysics subprogram focuses on high-impact science with proton-rich and neutron-rich nuclei and searches for super-heavy elements and nuclear processes that inform our understanding of stellar nucleosynthesis, neutron stars, and Big Bang nucleosynthesis. Both frontiers are identified in A New Era of Discovery: The 2023 Long Range Plan for Nuclear Science. The subfield of nuclear structure addresses the underlying nature of atomic nuclei and the limits of their existence and describes dynamical processes such as nuclear reactions and fission.
subtopics.title: (m) Nuclear Structure and Nuclear Astrophysics

subtopics.summary: https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/2280968/ This subprogram supports precision experiments to test the fundamental symmetries of nature and discover new particles and forces. These experiments address some of the most profound questions in physics today: What physical processes are responsible for the dominance of matter over antimatter in our universe? What is the fundamental nature of the neutrino, and is it its own antiparticle? What is the absolute mass of the neutrino?
subtopics.title: (n) Fundamental Symmetries

subtopics.summary: The Nuclear Data subprogram is multi-disciplinary with applications to energy, defense, space, and medicine. Nuclear data underlies modeling and simulation software in nuclear applications, so it is key for ensuring results are accurate. Working groups have been established among researchers, as well as Federal programs, to help coordinate, prioritize, and fund research efforts to improve nuclear data in basic science and applied nuclear technologies. In addition, the Nuclear Data subprogram collects, evaluates, and disseminates nuclear data with its support of the U.S.
subtopics.title: (o) Nuclear Data

subtopics.summary: Applications to this topic should be focused on basic research supporting novel or improved capabilities for inducing transmutation of atoms in targets to create radioisotopes that strongly align with the IRP mission space. This topic includes integrating AI and ML techniques to model and predict the purity and processing of radioisotopic products. Accelerator- and reactor-based isotope production have different considerations; applications to this topic can address either production modality.
subtopics.title: (a) Novel Isotopes and Production Routes

subtopics.summary: Applications to this topic should be focused on basic research supporting novel or improved aspects of targetry and target fabrication in a variety of form factors and batch sizes (e.g., milligrams to kilograms), low-loss advanced manufacturing techniques, as well as the development of innovative approaches, including integration of AI and ML techniques to model and predict the purity and processing of stable isotope products as well as the behavior of targets undergoing irradiation to optimize yield and minimize target failures during routine isotope production.
subtopics.title: (b) Targetry and Isotope Production Research

subtopics.subtopic_code: (c) Radio/Nuclear and Chemical Separation, Purification, and Synthesis
subtopics.summary: Work in this topic broadly applies to basic research supporting the improvement and/or development of novel chemical and physical processes to recover and purify radioisotopes from activated targets or further refinement and purification of stable isotope feedstocks and final products.
subtopics.title: (c) Radio/Nuclear and Chemical Separation, Purification, and Synthesis

subtopics.summary: Work in this topic should be focused on basic research supporting the development of isotopes that might be useful as biological tracers, imaging, or therapeutic agents. Developing or modifying chemical constructs which have physical or chemical properties that make them particularly useful with isotopes in this category would also be considered responsive. This topic includes modifying existing agents and synthesizing and developing novel ligands, pharmacokinetic modifying linkers, or other hydrodynamic volume altering compounds. IRP funds only basic science R&D.
subtopics.title: (d) Biological Tracers, Imaging, and Therapeutics

subtopics.summary: This area prioritizes technologies that enable rapid and effective construction, repair, and development of infrastructure in austere, contested, or damaged environments. Core interests span lightweight, multi-functional, and adaptable equipment suitable for diverse terrains; advanced construction and repair materials for rapid deployment and restoration; and automated or robotic systems to enhance speed and efficiency.
subtopics.title: Expeditionary Construction, Battle Damage Repair, and Advance Naval Base Construction Technologies

subtopics.summary: This area focuses on technologies that enable the rapid and sustained transfer of personnel, equipment, and supplies from ship to shore, particularly in austere or contested environments where traditional port infrastructure is limited or unavailable. Core interests include advanced amphibious connector craft and lighterage systems; modular and rapidly deployable causeways and piers; and automated cargo handling and transfer solutions that minimize beach time and maximize throughput.
subtopics.title: Logistics Over the Shore Technologies

subtopics.summary: Technologies that advance and sustain waterfront facilities in the harsh marine environment in the areas of cathodic protection, corrosion and weathering, metallurgy, concrete and pavements, and paints and coatings.
subtopics.title: Waterfront Facilities and Systems

subtopics.summary: Technologies for engineering, installing, and maintaining ocean and littoral underwater systems and magnetic silencing facilities. Advancements in physical and numerical modeling analysis, survey and route planning, procurement, installation and repair methods for critical fleet ranges, undersea surveillance and tactical communication facilities, undersea infrastructure, and power infrastructure. Advancements in geotechnical engineering regarding interactions with the seafloor and installed heavy load handling shipboard cabled sensor systems.
subtopics.title: Undersea Facilities & Systems

subtopics.summary: Technologies to advance the full lifecycle of Naval shore facilities and infrastructure from planning and design through construction, operations, maintenance, repair and disposal. Examples include advanced survey, planning, and design tools, alternative construction methods, industrialized construction, cathodic protection systems, corrosion & weathering, concrete & pavement materials, materials chemistry, materials testing, metallurgy, paints and coatings, roofing, structural modeling and analysis.
subtopics.title: Shore Facilities, Equipment & Systems

subtopics.summary: Technologies that advance energy security, efficiency, reliability, and resilience on Naval shore facilities and infrastructure. Unique program expertise includes: microgrid control systems, critical power applications, geothermal exploration and systems management, distributed energy resources, and alternatively fueled vehicles and infrastructure.
subtopics.title: Shore Energy Technology

subtopics.summary: Technologies to ensure the security and effectiveness of facilities infrastructure controls and expeditionary systems-related Information Technology (IT) and Operational Technology (OT) to mitigate cyber threats and resolve cybersecurity incidents.
subtopics.title: Facilities Related Control Systems Cybersecurity and Cyber Warfare

subtopics.summary: Technologies/methodologies for unencumbering military lands and reducing risk to human health including those to assess, manage, and/or remediate past releases of hazardous chemicals related to military operations, munitions and explosives of concern, material potentially presenting an explosive hazard, and chemicals of emerging concern in soil, soil covers, sediment, surface water, groundwater, and subsurface vapor.
subtopics.title: Installation Restoration, Munitions Response, and Groundwater Management

subtopics.summary: Technologies to ensure shore and marine-based regulatory compliance while minimizing operational environmental risks, constraints, and costs. Supports improved infrastructure reliability, resilience and mission capability. Focus areas include water quality (drinking water, stormwater and wastewater, air quality, oil spill response, hazardous waste, and solid waste. Includes shore and marine water resources management approaches for securing water availability, including water supply, usage, infrastructure, and delivery systems at installations.
subtopics.title: Installation Compliance and Water Resource Management

subtopics.summary: Develop, demonstrate, and assess information and technology solutions that support U.S. Navy’s at-sea compliance and permitting for legally protected marine species. Navy driven research needs support the ability to conduct uninterrupted at-sea training and testing, which preserves core Navy readiness capabilities. Focus areas include data to support the Navy Acoustic Effects Model (NAEMO), data processing and analysis tools, monitoring and mitigation technology demonstrations, and standards and metrics development.
subtopics.title: Living Marine Resources

subtopics.summary: Technologies that advance energy generation, storage, management, and distribution in the marine environment (including surface and undersea) to provide for persistent surveillance, autonomous vehicle recharging, communications nodes, or other applications where legacy methods of power delivery are not available or are significantly limited. For additional details on NAVFAC EXWC see our command website: https://exwc.navfac.navy.mil/
subtopics.title: Marine Energy Development

subtopics.summary: Physical Security and Asset Tracking technology for large facilities and expeditionary applications. Lightweight, forced entry resistant security containers and related technology for intermodal, expeditionary and special Missions. Development of advanced finite element and physical modeling to show proof of concept or test validation of different physical security systems. This can include both physical security systems as well as mechanical, energetic and ballistic threats.
subtopics.title: Physical Security, Locks and Barriers.
